ANOMALIE RESIDUE E ALTERAZIONI DELLA CURVATURA DEL FUSTO ➰

Questa sezione raggruppa difetti acquisiti da trauma meccanico (annodamento) e anomalie congenite che alterano la geometria trasversale o la curvatura del fusto, influenzandone la pettinabilità e l'aspetto estetico senza necessariamente indurre fragilità da frattura.

Triconodòsi (Capello Annodato / Trichonodosis)

Definizione:
Anomalia esclusivamente acquisita caratterizzata dalla formazione di veri e propri nodi lungo il fusto (single-strand knots). A livello della spira del nodo, la tensione meccanica causa lo sfaldamento della cuticola con esposizione e sfilacciamento della corteccia.
Patogenesi e Biomeccanica:
Deriva da traumi meccanici ripetuti (spazzolatura aggressiva, frizione). La sezione trasversale fortemente appiattita o ellittica riduce il momento d'inerzia alla torsione (ossia la resistenza strutturale del capello ad avvitarsi su se stesso), favorendo l'arricciamento autogeno e l'annodamento ("effetto molla").
Fattori di Rischio:
Prevalente in chi ha capelli ricci, crespi o molto fini (etnia africana o capelli caucasici ricci). Raramente spontanea in capelli estremamente lunghi e trascurati.

Sindrome dei Capelli Impettinabili (Uncombable Hair Syndrome - UHS)

Quadro clinico pediatrico correlato al segno microscopico dei Pili trianguli et canaliculi (fusti a sezione triangolare con una scanalatura longitudinale), con graduale risoluzione spontanea durante la pubertà.

Eziologia Molecolare e Cascata Biochimica UHS

Pathway Genetico

Patologia genetica ad eredità autosomica recessiva legata a mutazioni nel complesso di cheratinizzazione follicolare: PADI3, TGM3, TCHH e SULT2B1.

Fase 1: Deimina della Tricoialina
PADI3 → TCHH
La peptidilarginina deiminasi 3 (PADI3) deimina la tricoialina (TCHH), permettendone il legame con i filamenti di cheratina.
↓
Fase 2: Legami Crociati Isopeptidici
TGM3 (Transglutaminasi 3)
Catalizza i legami crociati isopeptidici stabili per il consolidamento strutturale.
↓
Esito Patologico
Cheratinizzazione Prematura IRS
Il difetto dell'asse provoca la cheratinizzazione prematura della guaina epiteliale interna (IRS - Inner Root Sheath), deformatrice e rigidificante sul fusto malleabile.

Correlato Clinico: Capelli secchi, disordinati e proiettati verso l'esterno, impossibili da appiattire ma privi di un significativo incremento della fragilità alla trazione.

Capelli Lanosi (Woolly Hair)

Morfologia e Diagnosi Differenziale:
Fusti con sezione ovoidale/appiattita, caratterizzati da torsioni assiali strette e curvature irregolari. Rispetto ai Pili Torti (torsioni di 180° lungo l'asse longitudinale), le torsioni si presentano meno strutturate e la resistenza meccanica del capello è ampiamente conservata.
Fisiopatologia:
Marcata riduzione della fase anagen (fase di crescita attiva, con lunghezza massima del capello spesso < 5 cm). L'impossibilità di pettinaggio è legata alla densità spaziale delle micro-curvature e non a frattura del fusto.
Variante ClinicaEreditarietà & GeneticaCaratteristiche Patologiche & Associazioni
Ereditaria (Generalizzata)Autosomica Dominante o RecessivaCoinvolge l'intero cuoio capelluto. Le forme recessive sono marcatore di sindromi cardio-cutanee gravemente invalidanti (es. Sindrome di Naxos o di Carvajal per mutazioni nei geni desmosomiali JUP o DSP).
Localizzata (Woolly Hair Nevus)Non ereditariaChiazza circoscritta su cuoio capelluto sano; talvolta presente in mosaicismo associato a nevi epidermici.
Acquisita (Kinky Hair indotto)Iatrogena / ReattivaRara, secondaria a farmaci (retinoidi sistemici quali acitretina/isotretinoina, inibitori di EGFR) o nelle fasi iniziali di alopecia androgenetica.

SEBORREA E DISFUNZIONE SEBACEA 💧

La seborrea è definita come un'aumentata produzione quantitativa di sebo (seborrea oleosa) o un'alterazione qualitativa della sua composizione lipidica (seborrea sicca). Non è una patologia stante a sé, bensì una disfunzione omeostatica che altera il film idrolipidico di superficie, creando un microambiente idoneo allo sviluppo di acne, forfora e dermatite seborroica.

Classificazione Clinica della Seborrea

Forma ClinicaMeccanismo FisiopatologicoManifestazioni Cutanee & Conseguenze
Seborrea FisiologicaAttività secretoria bilanciata delle ghiandole olocrine regolata da età, sesso, ormoni e genetica.Costituzione della barriera idrolipidica e lubrificazione fisiologica del fusto.
Seborrea Patologica (Oleosa)Iperproduzione quantitativa di sebo.Cute e annessi iper-untuosi, ritenzione sebacea (stasi di sebo ossidato), comedoni e disbiosi (alterazione dell'equilibrio ecologico) del microbiota.
Seborrea SeccaAlterazione qualitativa della frazione lipidica: deficit di acido linoleico ed eccesso di squalene perossidato.Aspetto desquamativo e xerotico (secchezza cutanea patologica), pur in presenza di normo o ipersecrezione ghiandolare.

Fisiopatologia e Meccanismi Molecolari

Cascata Molecolare della Seborrea

Endocrinologia & Microbioma
Stimolo Endocrino
Testosterone → DHT
Sintesi di 5α-diidrotestosterone via 5α-reduttasi di tipo I. Il DHT si lega al recettore androgeno (AR).
Potenziamento Signaling
IGF-1 / Insulina
Attivazione dell'asse mTORC1 che amplifica e co-stimola il pathway lipogenico.
↓
Attivazione Genica
Pathway SREBP-1c
Trascrizione della Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein per la stimolazione diretta della lipogenesi nei sebociti.
Alterazione Lipidica & Perossidazione:
Deplezione di acido linoleico (essenziale per la funzione barriera e la coesione intercheratinocitaria) e aumento relativo di squalene. Lo squalene perossidato (squalene monoidroperossido) induce uno stato pro-infiammatorio e ipercheratosi infundibolare (ispessimento del colletto del follicolo).
Ruolo del Microbiota e Malassezia spp.:
I lieviti lipofili opportunisti Malassezia restricta e M. globosa metabolizzano i trigliceridi sebacei tramite lipasi extracellulari, rilasciando acidi grassi liberi irritanti (es. acido oleico). Penetrazione nello strato corneo con conseguente infiammazione, prurito e desquamazione reattiva.

Conseguenze Cliniche e Diagnosi Differenziale

  • Alopecia Androgenetica: La seborrea agisce da cofattore: la microinfiammazione perifollicolare accelerata dai perossidi lipidici e dal microbiota amplifica la miniaturizzazione dei follicoli suscettibili.
  • Follicolite e Acne Volgare: L'ostruzione del microcomedone crea un ambiente anossico ideale per l'iperproliferazione di Cutibacterium acnes con conseguente cascata infiammatoria.
  • Pitiriasi Steatoide: Condizione intermedia caratterizzata da squame giallastre, unte e aderenti al cuoio capelluto, imbibite di sebo degradato.
  • Dermatite Seborroica: Dermatite cronica recidivante (eritema, desquamazione e prurito) localizzata nelle aree a maggiore densità sebacea, sostenuta dall'interazione tra sebo, Malassezia e risposta immunitaria dell'ospite.

Approccio Terapeutico e Sebo-Regolazione

Il target clinico prevede la riduzione del carico microbico, il ripristino del turnover epidermico e il controllo della lipogenesi, salvaguardando l'integrità della barriera cutanea per prevenire l'effetto rebound (ipersecrezione reattiva compensatoria).

Classe TerapeuticaPrincipi AttiviMeccanismo d'Azione Clinico
Antifungini & AntimicrobiciKetoconazolo / Ciclopirox Olamina
Piroctone Olamina / Zinco Piritione		Ampio spettro contro Malassezia spp.; azione citostatica (blocco della proliferazione cellulare) e normalizzante sul microbiota cutaneo.
Cheratolitici & Sebo-ModulatoriAcido Salicilico / Acido Azelaico
Zinco PCA / Niacinamide		Azione lipofila cheratolitica (rimozione dei tappi cornei), antinfiammatoria, inibizione della 5α-reduttasi e protezione dalla perossidazione dello squalene.
Supporto Fisioterapico & StrumentaleAlta Frequenza
LLLT (Photobiomodulation)		Generazione di ozono ad azione battericida, fungicida e vasomodulante; laser a bassa intensità (LLLT - Low-Level Laser Therapy) per attenuare l'infiammazione e stimolare la riparazione.

FORFORA (PITIRIASIS SIMPLEX CAPITIS) 🌨️

La forfora è una condizione cronica non infiammatoria (o levemente infiammatoria) caratterizzata da desquamazione visibile del cuoio capelluto. È causata da un accelerato turnover epidermico: il tempo di ricambio dei cheratinociti si riduce da circa 28 giorni a 2–7 giorni. Le cellule non raggiungono la completa maturazione e si aggregano in squame visibili prima di distaccarsi.

Fisiopatologia: Triade Eziologica e Danno di Barriera

Triade Eziopatogenetica della Forfora

Homeostasis Barrier
1. Eccesso di Sebo (Substrato) + 2. Presenza di Malassezia + 3. Suscettibilità Individuale
La patogenesi richiede l'interazione simultanea di tutti e tre i fattori (genetica, assetto immunitario e integrità della barriera).
Ruolo della Malassezia:
La forfora richiede la presenza del lievito lipofilo Malassezia (specie M. globosa e M. restricta). Le sue lipasi idrolizzano i trigliceridi del sebo rilasciando acidi grassi liberi (es. acido oleico). Nei soggetti suscettibili, l'acido oleico penetra nello strato corneo, inducendo irritazione, infiammazione sub-clinica e paracheratosi (persistenza dei nuclei cellulari nello strato corneo dovuta a iperproliferazione).
Alterazione della Barriera Cutanea:
Lo strato corneo forforaico presenta una funzione barriera compromessa e una maggiore permeabilità (TEWL aumentato - Transepidermal Water Loss, o perdita d'acqua transepidermica). Questo favorisce la penetrazione di agenti irritanti e la disidratazione, alimentando un circolo vizioso di secchezza e desquamazione.

Classificazione Clinica della Forfora

VarianteMorfologia delle SquameStato della Cute SottostanteInquadramento Clinico
Pitiriasi Secca (Semplice)Fini, bianche o grigiastre, polverulente e poco aderenti.Normale o lievemente xerotica (secca). Prurito leve o assente.Tipica della stagione invernale (aria secca).
Pitiriasi Grassa (Steatoide)Grosse, untuose e giallastre, aggregate in placche aderenti.Eritematosa (arrossata), oleosa e infiammata.Forma lieve di dermatite seborroica; richiede un trattamento più aggressivo.

Strategia Terapeutica e Gestione

L'obiettivo terapeutico è controllare la popolazione di Malassezia, normalizzare il turnover cheratinocitario e ridurre l'infiammazione, ripristinando la barriera cutanea.

Categoria FarmacologicaPrincipi AttiviMeccanismo d'Azione Specifico
Agenti Antimicotici- Ketoconazolo (2%)
- Piritione di Zinco (ZPT)
- Ciclopirox Olamina / Solfuro di Selenio		Inibizione della sintesi dell'ergosterolo (componente della membrana fungina); attività fungicida, antibatterica e citostatica per ridurre l'iperproliferazione dei cheratinociti.
Agenti Cheratolitici- Acido Salicilico
- Zolfo		Favoriscono la desquamazione chimica ("scollamento" delle squame) e la penetrazione follicolare; azione sebostatica. Non hanno attività antimicotica diretta.
Coadiuvanti NaturaliTea Tree Oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)Attività antifungina dimostrata in studi clinici contro le specie di Malassezia.

Correttezza d'Uso e Parametri Chimico-Fisici

Protocollo D'Uso

È fondamentale utilizzare shampoo con un pH acido (4.0–5.5) per rispettare il mantello idrolipidico fisiologico e creare un ambiente sfavorevole alla proliferazione fungina (che preferisce pH neutri o alcalini).

Il tempo di contatto è cruciale: lo shampoo terapeutico deve agire per 3–5 minuti prima del risciacquo. Studi dimostrano che un contatto inferiore a 2 minuti riduce drasticamente l'efficacia antimicotica e citostatica dei principi attivi.

CAPELLI: COME SONO FATTI E IL LORO CICLO VITALE

1. ANATOMIA E STRUTTURA DEL CAPELLO

I peli e i capelli sono filamenti fatti di cheratina. Nascono da un "sacco" nella pelle chiamato FOLLICOLO PILIFERO.

Il follicolo si trova sotto la pelle del cuoio capelluto (derma). La sua parte finale, concava, si chiama BULBO.

La lunghezza, lo spessore e la posizione dei capelli cambiano in base a dove si trovano, al sesso, all'età e alla razza.

Le Parti del Capello

  • La parte che esce dalla pelle si chiama FUSTO (o STELO).
  • La parte sotto la pelle (dentro il follicolo) si chiama RADICE.
  • In fondo alla radice c'è la PAPILLA DERMICA. Questa papilla porta il nutrimento al capello.
  • Tra il bulbo e la radice c'è la MATRICE DEL CAPELLO. La matrice crea tutti i componenti del capello.

Queste parti formano l'APPARATO PILOSEBACEO.

APPARATO PILOSEBACEO: COMPONENTI

  • ▶ FOLLICOLO PILIFERO (con il capello)
  • ▶ MUSCOLO PILO ERETTORE
  • ▶ GHIANDOLA SEBACEA

FOLLICOLO PILIFERO:

Il follicolo è un "sacco" della pelle, inclinato, che scende nel derma per 1-3 mm. Contiene il pelo e le sue guaine.

Ogni persona ha circa 5 milioni di follicoli. Circa 100.000 sono sul cuoio capelluto. Questo numero è stabilito prima della nascita e non aumenta più.

GHIANDOLA SEBACEA:

Questa ghiandola produce il sebo, una sostanza grassa (trigliceridi, colesterolo, ecc.).

Il sebo serve a lubrificare, ammorbidire e proteggere il capello man mano che cresce. Il sebo si diffonde sulla pelle e sul capello. La sua attività è controllata da fattori ormonali e alimentari.

MUSCOLO PILO-ERETTORE:

È fatto di fibre muscolari lisce. Si attacca al follicolo.

Quando si contrae (per freddo o emozioni come paura), il pelo si mette dritto. Questo causa la pelle d'oca. Aiuta anche a far uscire il sebo.

2. STRUTTURA DEL CAPELLO

Il capello è una fibra complessa. Contiene acqua (10-30%) e grassi (sebo, cere, ecc.) per proteggersi.

Il fusto del capello ha tre strati:

  • CUTICOLA: È la parte più esterna. È fatta di cellule piatte e sovrapposte, come le tegole di un tetto.
  • CORTECCIA: Si trova sotto la cuticola. È la parte più grande del capello. Dà al capello la sua resistenza e contiene la melanina (colore).
  • MIDOLLO: È la parte centrale, quasi assente nel fusto.

Le molecole principali sono: cheratina (struttura), melanina (colore) e minerali.

CHERATINA: LA STRUTTURA FONDAMENTALE

Il capello è fatto principalmente di cheratina. Ne esistono due tipi:

  • Cheratina Filamentosa: Forma dei fasci (fibrille) nella corteccia.
  • Cheratina Amorfa: Riempie gli spazi tra i fasci, dando stabilità.

COME RIMANE STABILE LA STRUTTURA?

Le catene di cheratina sono unite da dei "ponti" che le tengono insieme. Ci sono 3 tipi di ponti:

1. PONTI IDROGENO

Sono legami molto deboli. Si rompono facilmente con l'acqua o il calore. Danno al capello flessibilità.

2. PONTI SALINI

Sono legami mediamente forti. Si rompono con forte calore o con sostanze acide/basiche. Danno al capello resistenza.

3. PONTI DISOLFURO

Sono legami molto forti (legami covalenti), fatti da atomi di zolfo.

Questi ponti danno struttura (ad esempio i capelli ricci naturali). Possono essere rotti solo con molta energia (es. trattamenti chimici).

I tre tipi di legame contribuiscono tutti alla resistenza del capello.

MINERALI

I minerali sono essenziali. Se mancano, i capelli diventano fragili, secchi e opachi.

I minerali più importanti sono:

  • FERRO: Se manca, causa fragilità e caduta eccessiva.
  • RAME: Fondamentale per il colore (melanina) e per i ponti disolfuro.
  • ZINCO: Indispensabile per la crescita delle cellule.

LIPIDI (GRASSI)

I lipidi provengono per lo più dal sebo.

I fosfolipidi sono importanti perché aiutano a mantenere la corretta idratazione del capello.

MELANINE: IL COLORE NATURALE

La melanina è il pigmento naturale. Si trova nella corteccia ed è prodotta dai melanociti.

I tipi di pigmento sono:

  • EUMELANINA: Colore blu/nero (capelli scuri).
  • FEOMELANINA: Colore giallo/rosso (capelli biondi e rossi).
  • TRICOCROMI: Pigmenti speciali per il colore rosso intenso.

La melanina nasce dall'aminoacido tirosina. La diversa percentuale dei pigmenti determina il colore finale del capello.

3. CICLO VITALE DEL CAPELLO

Il capello ha cicli di crescita e di riposo. Quando un capello vecchio cade, il follicolo ne forma uno nuovo.

Il ciclo ha 3 fasi:

1. ANAGEN: Fase di crescita

È la fase più lunga. La matrice del capello è molto attiva e lo fa crescere.

  • Durata: 2-4 anni nell'uomo, 3-7 anni nella donna.
  • Il capello cresce di circa 1-1,5 cm al mese.

2. CATAGEN: Fase di transizione

È molto breve, dura 2-4 settimane. La matrice smette di lavorare.

3. TELOGEN: Fase di riposo

È il periodo di riposo, dura circa 3 mesi.

Il capello cade solo quando ne sta crescendo uno nuovo che lo spinge fuori.

La caduta dei capelli nell'uomo è a "mosaico": ogni follicolo segue il suo ciclo da solo. Questo assicura che non ci siano periodi senza capelli.

Nota: ogni follicolo può fare fino a 30 cicli di vita.

en.hair_anatomy_section:
HAIR: ANATOMY, STRUCTURE AND LIFE CYCLE

Hair strands are filamentous cutaneous appendages of a keratinized nature (protein structures produced by the skin), originating from the HAIR FOLLICLES: oblique invaginations of the epidermis (inclined skin channels) that penetrate into the dermis (the deep middle layer), terminating at their base in an expanded and concave structure, the HAIR BULB. The morphology, topographic distribution, and thickness of the hair are determined by genetic, anatomical, hormonal, and ethnic factors.

Anatomically, the pilosebaceous unit is divided into three distinct portions: the SHAFT (or STEM), the visible segment emerged on the skin surface; the ROOT, the intra-follicular portion; and the BULB, the deep basal portion. Inside the bulbous cavity resides the DERMAL PAPILLA, a conical, highly vascularized, and innervated connective structure (rich in blood vessels and nerve endings), essential for the nourishment and regulation of the follicular cycle.

The lower portion of the bulb wrapping around the papilla constitutes the HAIR MATRIX (germinative layer). This population of undifferentiated cells with high mitotic activity (unspecialized cells that divide and multiply rapidly) is responsible for protein synthesis and progressive keratinization (the hardening and maturation process of keratin) that generates all components of the hair.

The combination of the follicle, the hair, and adjacent glandular and muscular structures constitutes the morpho-functional unit known as the PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT, whose proper functioning ensures the integrity of the skin barrier and the homeostasis (the ideal physiological balance) of the tissue.

The PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT comprises three fundamental structures:

  • The HAIR FOLLICLE, containing the hair strand or hair and its relative sheaths.
  • The ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLE.
  • The SEBACEOUS GLAND (which, in certain locations, is associated with an apocrine sweat gland).
STRUCTUREDESCRIPTION AND PHYSIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
HAIR FOLLICLEIt is a specialized epidermal structure, oriented obliquely relative to the skin surface, extending into the dermis down to a depth of 1-3 mm. The total number of follicles in humans is genetically determined (approximately 5 million), with about 100,000 located on the scalp. Follicular morphogenesis (the formation of follicles during fetal growth) is an early process: it begins between the 9th and 12th week of gestation and is completed by the 7th month of fetal life; subsequently, no new follicles are formed de novo (no new hair follicles are ever formed after birth).
SEBACEOUS GLANDIt is a holocrine exocrine gland (a gland that pours its secretion outward by completely dissolving its own cells) that secretes sebum into the neck of the hair follicle via the sebaceous duct. Sebum, a lipid mixture rich in triglycerides, squalene, waxes, and cholesterol, lubricates, moisturizes, and waterproofs the cuticle, protecting the skin. Located in the upper portion (infundibulum, i.e., the channel exit) of the follicle, its activity does not interfere with the mitotic processes (cell division) of the bulbous matrix. Sebaceous secretion is regulated by endocrine factors (mainly androgen hormones), as well as nervous and metabolic stimuli.
ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLEConsisting of a bundle of smooth muscle fibers (involuntary musculature), it anchors to the papillary dermis and inserts onto the connective sheath of the follicle, just above the sebaceous gland. Its involuntary contraction, mediated by the sympathetic nervous system in response to cold or emotional stimuli (fear, stress), causes the verticalization of the hair shaft (goosebumps or piloerection). This movement exerts mechanical pressure on the underlying sebaceous gland, actively favoring the expulsion of sebum into the follicular lumen (channel).

THE PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT IN DETAIL - HAIR STRUCTURE:

Hair is a complex biological structure with a high degree of organization, consisting of specific macromolecular and chemical components. Its hydration rate ranges from 10% to 30% by weight, closely related to environmental thermo-hygrometric conditions (air temperature and humidity). The cuticular surface is coated with a lipid film of sebum (composed of triglycerides, waxes, cholesterol, phospholipids, and squalene) that performs an essential barrier function against external chemical and physical insults.

The hair shaft is structured in three concentric layers:

  • Cuticle: outermost layer, formed by flattened and strongly keratinized cells (up to 6-8 overlapping layers), arranged longitudinally like roof tiles to protect the underlying cortex.
  • Cortex: located beneath the cuticle, it constitutes the quantitatively largest component of the shaft. It is formed by fusiform (spindle-shaped or elongated) cells rich in aligned keratin filaments, determining the mechanical properties of strength and elasticity of the hair. It houses melanin granules, responsible for pigmentation (natural color).
  • Medulla: central column of the shaft, often discontinuous or absent in fine hair. It consists of loosely connected keratinized cells (joined in a low-density manner), arranged in rows and interspersed with air vacuoles (microspaces containing air) and traces of pigment.
en.hair_biochemistry:
In summary: The molecular structure of hair is supported by a complex keratin matrix, stabilized by high- and low-energy chemical bonds that determine its elasticity and shape. The balance between lipids and essential trace elements preserves hydration and mechanical resistance, while follicular melanogenesis regulates natural pigmentation and protection against oxidative stress.

BIOCHEMISTRY OF HAIR

From a biochemical standpoint, the fundamental constituents of hair (aside from water) include keratin (predominantly in hydrophobic α-conformation, a high-resistance protein structure that repels water), structural and surface lipids, melanin pigments (eumelanins and pheomelanins), and a fraction of atomic-state essential trace elements and minerals (such as iron, zinc, magnesium, and calcium).

KERATIN AND ULTRASTRUCTURE

Hair keratins are of two types, classified according to their structural characteristics as filamentous keratin and amorphous protein matrix. Filamentous keratin forms a complex ultrastructure organized into bundles or fibrils in the cortex, while the amorphous protein matrix fills the empty spaces between the fibrils, stabilizing their architecture. Polypeptide chains (chains of linked amino acids) coil upon themselves assuming a spiral shape similar to DNA.

Keratin macromolecules, consisting of long polypeptide chains, are stabilized and cohesively bound laterally thanks to interchain chemical bonds (bridges) established between amino acid residues of adjacent filaments.

Types of chemical bonds in keratin and their impact on physiological resistance
Bond TypeNature and SensitivityPhysiological Role and Characteristics
Hydrogen BondsREF #9
Weak electrostatic interactions, easily cleaved by the action of water and heat (forming the basis of temporary thermal styling).Established between the carbonyl oxygen atom (-C=O) and the amide hydrogen (-NH-) of the peptide backbone. Intrachain bonds stabilize the α-helix, while interchain bonds confer flexibility and reversible elasticity.
Salt Bridges (Ionic Interactions)REF #9
Medium-energy bonds, sensitive to extreme temperature changes and sudden pH shifts (acidic or basic solutions).Electrostatic interactions between ionized side chains of acidic amino acids (glutamic acid, aspartic acid) and basic amino acids (lysine, arginine). Numerically very high, they are essential for tensile strength.
Disulfide BondsREF #9
Strong covalent bonds (irreversible with water/heat alone), formed by the oxidation of thiol groups (-SH) of cysteine to form cystine (-S-S-).Main stabilization factor of tertiary and quaternary structure. They determine rigidity, permanent shape (curl), and chemical-physical resistance. Require redox chemical treatments (straightening, perms).

Although salt and hydrogen bonds have lower binding energy, their extremely high numerical density means that each of the three classes contributes approximately 1/3 to the overall mechanical strength and shape stability of the hair.

The spatial configuration, density, and geometric regularity with which these bonds are distributed (particularly the architecture of disulfide bonds) determine the macro-molecular organization of the cortex and, consequently, the morphological phenotype (straight, wavy, curly) of the hair.

TRACE ELEMENTS AND MINERALS

Minerals constitute essential biochemical and catalytic components for hair homeostasis (metabolic equilibrium). Mineral deficiency states alter keratogenesis (keratin synthesis), inducing brittleness, dryness, loss of luster, and follicular cycle abnormalities (telogen effluvium or excessive shedding).

Quantitative breakdown and clinical-biochemical role of major minerals in the hair shaft
Trace ElementConcentrationBiochemical and Clinical Function
Iron4 - 12 μg/gEssential enzymatic cofactor; deficiency (sideropenia) compromises bulb matrix proliferation causing weakening. Particularly concentrated in red hair (pheomelanin).
Magnesium30 - 45 μg/gActivator in enzymatic complexes and ATP synthesis (cellular energy molecule), fundamental for protein biosynthesis. Highly present in dark hair.
Copper16 - 50 μg/gCatalytic core of the tyrosinase enzyme, essential for melanogenesis (color production). Participates in catalyzing disulfide bond formation.
Zinc150 - 180 μg/gFundamental trace element for polymerase activity and cell division in the bulb. Chronic deficiency inhibits cell turnover causing shaft brittleness and dystrophy.

The endogenous mineral component regulates the intrinsic hydration of the hair fiber through hygroscopic equilibrium (the ability to retain moisture); bound water loss alters macrofibril arrangement, compromising structural cohesion.

STRUCTURAL AND SURFACE LIPIDS

REF #3

Lipids are divided into exogenous (of sebaceous origin: triglycerides, waxes, squalene, free fatty acids coating the cuticle) and endogenous (structural lipids integrated into the cell membrane and CMC - Cell Membrane Complex, such as cholesterol and cholesterol sulfate).

Of fundamental structural relevance are phospholipids and ceramides, intrinsic constituents of cell membranes. Thanks to their amphipathic nature (ability to bind both water and fats), they modulate hydrophobicity and permeability, regulating water flows and ensuring hydration, elasticity, and intercellular cohesion between cuticular and cortical cells.

MELANINS AND CHROMATIC PHENOTYPE

REF #4

Melanin is the natural pigmented polymer localized predominantly in the cortex. It is synthesized within melanosomes (specialized organelles) by melanocytes in the hair bulb. The concentration and ratio between these polymers determine the natural chromatic spectrum (canities or graying is due to the cessation of melanogenesis).

Dark Pigment
Eumelanin
→ Brown and black tones
Insoluble high-molecular-weight polymer, localized in large ellipsoidal melanosomes. Absorbs the light spectrum, protecting the fiber from photodamage.
Light Pigment
Pheomelanin
→ Blonde and red tones
Sulfur-containing polymer with spherical and dispersed melanosomes. Reflects yellow/orange tones conferring warm shades to the chromatic scale.
Rutilus VariantREF #4
Rutilus Phenotype and MC1R Genetics
→ Natural red hair and genetic regulation
Natural red hair is caused by a predominance of pheomelanin (red-yellow-sulfur pigment) over eumelanin. The phenotype is determined by recessive loss-of-function genetic variants of the MC1R gene (chromosome 16), which reduce receptor activity and block eumelanin synthesis, favoring the pheomelanin metabolic pathway.

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Biosynthesis of Melanins (Melanogenesi)

REF #4 DOI

The common precursor of the metabolic pathway is the amino acid L-tyrosine. In eumelanin synthesis, tyrosine is hydroxylated into L-DOPA and oxidized to dopaquinone by the action of tyrosinase (a copper-dependent metalloprotein enzyme). Through sequential stages of cyclization and oxidative polymerization, dopaquinone evolves into insoluble macromolecules. Catalytic efficiency determines the final pigment intensity.

The synthesis of pheomelanin occurs in the presence of a critical concentration of cysteine (or glutathione): cysteine binds to dopaquinone forming cysteinyl-DOPA, which generates yellow-orange pigments through subsequent oxidations.

Oculocutaneous albinism represents the primary pathological model of this pathway: mutations in the tyrosinase gene alter the tertiary structure of the enzyme, inhibiting tyrosine conversion and resulting in the total absence of pigment synthesis.

The reciprocal percentage variation and volumetric density of these fractions genetically define the entire scale of tones and shades of natural hair.
en.life_cycle_section:
THE LIFE CYCLE OF THE HAIR FOLLICLE

The hair follicle is a dynamic organ characterized by asynchronous cyclic activity (where each hair follows its own independent rhythm), alternating between growth, regression, and rest phases. Under physiological conditions, the shedding of an element in the telogen phase coincides with the activation of a new cycle in anagen within the same follicle. Phenomena of poliotrichia (presence of multiple hair shafts emerging from a single ostium or pore) occur predominantly in scalp follicular units, where multiple distinct follicles share a sebaceous gland and a common pilary canal.

The biological life cycle of hair is classically divided into three main phases: anagen, catagen, and telogen.

Growth phase (ANAGEN):

Anagen is divided into 6 sub-phases (from anagen I to anagen VI). The biological process begins with the activation of stem cells in the bulge niche (the follicular swelling zone acting as a regenerative reservoir) and the matrix, which stimulate intense mitotic activity (cell replication) until the complete formation of the new shaft. At the scalp level, the anagen phase has an average duration of 2–4 years in men and 3–7 years in women. Consequently, the loss of the "mature" hair is compensated by the genesis of a new terminal filament. In other body regions, anagen is drastically shorter: 1–6 months for eyelashes and 20–40 days for limb vellus hair.

The duration of anagen is genetically determined and regulates the maximum reachable length of the hair, whose kinetic growth rate is approximately 1–1.5 cm per month, with rates generally higher in females. This phase shows variations according to ethnicity (being maximal in lissotrichous hair, i.e., straight and circular in section, typical of Asian ethnicity) and scalp topography: follicles in the occipital region (nape) exhibit a longer anagen compared to temporal ones. At the same time, the rate of vertical proliferation is statistically higher at the vertex compared to the nape.

In follicles affected by androgenetic defluvium (common baldness), there is a progressive temporal reduction of anagen (down to only 3–5 months), associated with the phenomenon of follicular miniaturization, which limits the shaft length to a few centimeters and alters its structure into vellus hair (a thin, faded, and medulla-free hair). Biological aging (chronological aging) also physiologically reduces anagen duration and shaft diameter.

Scientific Note

REF #2

The replicative potential of the follicle is not mathematically predetermined at a local level, but is constrained by the stem cell reserve and organism longevity. Over an average human lifespan, a single follicle completes approximately 25–30 cycles before undergoing senescence.

Summary of hair biological cycle phases, biological state, duration, and key characteristics
Cycle PhaseBiological StateAverage Duration (Scalp)Key Characteristic
ANAGENActive growth2–4 years (Men) / 3–7 years (Women)Intense mitotic activity and keratin synthesis.
CATAGENInvolution / Apoptosis2–4 weeksCessation of pigmentation and ascent of the dermal papilla.
TELOGENMetabolic restAbout 3 monthsFormation of the "club" bulb waiting for expulsion.
EXOGENActive sheddingFinal phase of TelogenEnzymatic process of shaft expulsion from the follicle.
KENOGENLatency / Empty follicleVariable (physiological or pathological)Time interval between shedding and new anagen.

Phase of involution and apoptosis (CATAGEN):

It is a transitory involutive phase lasting 2–4 weeks. During catagen, matrix keratinocytes undergo programmed apoptosis (a form of controlled cellular suicide), melanin synthesis stops, and the lower portion of the follicle resorbs, causing the dermal papilla to ascend toward the upper layers of the dermis (bulge zone).

Phase of functional rest and expulsion (TELOGEN and EXOGEN):

Telogen represents the period of metabolic quiescence (functional rest) of the follicle, with an average duration of about 3 months. Mitotic activity is absent and the anchoring sheaths keratinize, giving the hair base the typical "club" structure. The actual detachment of the shaft from the follicle (now classified independently as the exogen phase) is an active process regulated by proteolytic enzymes that degrade the junction between hair and follicle, often facilitated by the mechanical push of the new filament in anagen, thus ensuring the continuity of hair turnover (natural hair replacement).

If the follicle remains empty for a latent period between the shedding of the old hair and the start of the new anagen, it is termed the kenogen phase. This empty interval, although present in a minimal percentage in the healthy scalp, undergoes a significant and pathological increase in androgenetic alopecia.

The traumatic or mechanical extraction of a hair in telogen induces a biochemical signal that interrupts follicle quiescence, stimulating the early start of a new anagen. The characteristic whitish swelling visible at the base of spontaneously shed hairs is not the "vital root", but rather the keratinized and pigment-free bulb typical of the telogen phase.

Unlike many mammals subject to synchronous molting (where hairs fall out all together), hair replacement in humans occurs according to an asynchronous "mosaic" pattern: each follicle evolves independently of adjacent ones. Systemic fluctuations and photoperiod variations (hours of sunlight) can nevertheless induce partial follicle synchronization, clinically evident as physiological seasonal effluvium (temporary increase in shedding) during transition seasons (autumn and spring).

Strictly from a cyto-functional profile (relative to cell behavior and function), follicle activity is divided into two macro-phases:

  • A proliferative and morphogenetic phase: characterized by the rapid downward extension of the keratinocytic column invading the deep dermis, corresponding to the initial sub-phases of anagen (from anagen I to anagen V);
  • A differentiative and synthetic phase: predominant during anagen VI, where mitotic activity stabilizes at the basal level necessary to sustain continuous keratinization and shaft protein synthesis. Subsequent catagen represents mitotic arrest with terminal differentiation of residual cells, while telogen constitutes the biosynthetic silence necessary for structural reorganization of the follicular unit.

The temporal heterogeneity of the pilary cycle in different anatomical areas (e.g., inverted anagen/telogen ratio in the pubis and eyebrows compared to the scalp) justifies the different biological length of body hairs and explains the selective susceptibility of follicles to specific dermatoses and immune or hormone-dependent pathologies.
en.atomic_structure_bonds:
THE ATOM AND CHEMICAL BONDS ⚛️

The atom is the smallest particle of a chemical element that retains its specific characteristics and identity.

Main Components

It consists of:

Center of Mass
Nucleus
→ Protons and Neutrons
Composed of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (uncharged). Concentrates almost all the mass of the atom (>99.9%).
Electron Cloud
Electrons
→ Quantum Mechanical Model
Negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus occupying orbitals, regions of space where the probability of finding them is maximum.

Fundamental Concept

Neutral State
Charge Balance
An electrically neutral atom has a number of protons equal to the number of electrons, resulting in a net charge = 0.

Ions 🧪

An ION is an atom (or group of atoms) that has lost or gained one or more electrons, acquiring a net electrical charge.

Electron Acquisition
Anion
→ Negative Charge (-)
Formed by the acquisition of electrons by the atom; the resulting electrical charge is net and negative.
Electron Loss
Cation
→ Positive Charge (+)
Formed by the loss of electrons by the atom; the resulting electrical charge is net and positive.

Periodic Table of Elements 📊

Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number (Z), according to the periodicity principle formulated by Mendeleev in 1869.

Box Contents

Periodic Table
Structure of the Standard Box
  1. In the center: the chemical symbol (e.g., Na, Cl).
  2. Highlighted: the atomic number Z (number of protons; defines the element's identity).
  3. At the bottom: the relative atomic mass (expressed in u, unified atomic mass unit; it is the weighted average of the masses of its natural isotopes).

Chemical Bonds and Stability 🔗

Atoms interact to achieve a state of minimum potential energy, forming more stable aggregates.

Guiding Principle
Spontaneity of Bonding
The bond forms spontaneously because the resulting system has a lower energy content than isolated atoms. Lower potential energy = greater stability.

Lewis Theory and Valency

Atoms interact to achieve a stable external electronic configuration (minimum energy), often similar to that of noble gases.

The Octet Rule

Noble gases (group 18) are chemically inert because they possess a complete valence shell: 8 electrons (octet), except for helium which is stable with 2 (duet).

Rule: “Atoms tend to lose, gain, or share electrons to achieve the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas (8 electrons in the outer shell, or 2 for H and He).”

Scientific note: This rule is an excellent approximation for periods 2 and 3 elements, but presents exceptions (e.g., electron-deficient molecules, expanded octet in higher periods).

Bond Energy ⚡

Thermodynamic Parameter
Bond Energy and Bond Length
Bond energy is the minimum energy required to break one mole of chemical bonds in the gaseous state (kJ/mol). High values indicate strong bonds and thermodynamically stable molecules. Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of bonded atoms.

STRONG BONDS (INTRAMOLECULAR) 🔩

1. Ionic Bond

Δχ ≥ 1.7
Electrostatic Attraction
→ Almost total electron transfer

Electrostatic force of attraction between ions of opposite charge. Formed typically between a metal and a non-metal with high electronegativity difference.

Formation Mechanism:
  1. Transfer of valence electrons between atoms.
  2. The less electronegative atom loses electrons (becomes a cation).
  3. The more electronegative atom gains electrons (becomes an anion).

Does not form isolated molecules, but ordered three-dimensional structures called crystal lattices (e.g., NaCl).

2. Covalent Bond

Achieved through the sharing of electrons between non-metallic atoms with similar or identical electronegativity (Δχ < 1.7).

Types of Covalent Bonds:
Δχ ≤ 0.4
Pure Covalent (Nonpolar)
→ E.g., H₂, O₂, CH₄
Established between identical atoms or with negligible electronegativity difference. The electron cloud is distributed perfectly symmetrically between the two nuclei.
0.4 < Δχ < 1.7
Polar Covalent
→ E.g., HCl, H₂O
Electrons are attracted more strongly by the more electronegative atom, creating a partial negative charge (δ⁻) on it and a positive one (δ⁺) on the other, forming an electric dipole.
Coordination
Dative Covalent Bond
→ E.g., H₃O⁺, NH₄⁺ (Symbol: →)
The shared electron pair comes entirely from a single atom (donor, with lone pair) and is accommodated in an empty orbital of the other (acceptor). Once formed, it is indistinguishable from a simple covalent bond.

*Note: Exceptions to the octet rule exist, such as incomplete octet (e.g., Boron compounds), expanded octet (e.g., SF6), or molecules with an odd number of electrons.

3. Metallic Bond ⚙️

Drude-Lorentz Model
Sea of Electrons
Consisting of a geometric lattice of positive ions immersed in a diffused cloud of delocalized valence electrons free to move. Cohesion is guaranteed by omnidirectional electrostatic attraction between mobile electrons and ionic cores.

WEAK BONDS (Intermolecular Forces) 💧

Weak bonds have a bond energy significantly lower than interatomic (intramolecular) bonds, but they determine the macroscopic properties and physical state of compounds.

Van der Waals Interactions
Dipole-Dipole & Dispersions
Include dipole-dipole interactions (between polar molecules) and London dispersion forces (present in all molecules, but dominant among nonpolar ones).
20–25 kJ/mol
Hydrogen Bond
Very intense dipole-dipole interaction. Formed when hydrogen is bonded to small, electronegative atoms (F, O, N) and is attracted by nearby lone pairs.
Anomalous Behavior
The Hydrogen Bond in Water

In Ice: Forces molecules into a tetrahedral geometry (open hexagonal lattice), increasing volume and reducing density, allowing ice to float.

In Liquid Phase: Bonds continuously break and reform, conferring high cohesion, surface tension, and high phase transition points.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS, INORGANIC COMPOUNDS, AND MIXTURES 🧪⚗️

In summary: Chemical reactions and the classification of inorganic compounds describe the transformations and properties of matter based on molecular bonds and acid-base behavior. The study of dispersed and colloidal systems integrates formulative chemistry, distinguishing between homogeneous solutions and stable heterogeneous mixtures.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS: TYPES AND REPRESENTATION

A chemical reaction is a process in which chemical bonds are broken and/or formed, resulting in the redistribution of atoms and the transformation of reactants into products with different chemical properties.

Chemical Equation

The chemical equation is the qualitative and quantitative representation of a reaction, where reactants are written on the left and products on the right:

REACTANTS → PRODUCTS

Classification of Reactions (by Mechanism)

Scheme: A + B → AB
Synthesis
Two or more substances (elements or compounds) combine to form a single more complex compound.
Scheme: AB → A + B
Decomposition (Cleavage)
A compound splits into two or more simpler substances through energy input (thermolysis, electrolysis, or photolysis).
Scheme: A + BC → AC + B
Single Replacement (Displacement)
A free element, more reactive, substitutes and displaces another less reactive element present in a compound.
Scheme: AB + CD → AD + CB
Double Replacement
Two compounds in solution exchange their constituents (ions) to form new compounds (often with the formation of a precipitate, gas, or water).

Thermodynamics and Reversibility

Symbol: ⇌
Reversible Reactions
Dynamic equilibrium
Products react with each other to reform reactants, reaching a state where the rate of the forward reaction equals that of the reverse reaction.
Symbol: →
Irreversible Reactions
Unidirectional completion
They proceed almost entirely toward product formation until the limiting reactant is exhausted. Stable products do not spontaneously restore reactants.

INORGANIC COMPOUNDS 🔬

These are chemical substances typically characterized by the absence of carbon-hydrogen (C-H) bonds. Unlike organic compounds, most do not contain carbon; however, certain carbon-containing species (such as carbon oxides, carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, and cyanides) are classified as inorganic due to their chemical properties and behavior analogous to mineral salts.

Nomenclature, characteristics, and reactivity of major inorganic compound classes
Chemical ClassOrigin and ReactionNomenclature and Examples
Basic OxidesBinary compounds formed by a metal and oxygen.Name: Oxide of + [Metal].
Examples: ZnO (Zinc oxide), MgO (Magnesium oxide).
Acid Oxides (Anhydrides)Binary compounds formed by a non-metal and oxygen.Name: Anhydride + [Non-metal] + suffix / IUPAC: Oxide of + prefix.
Examples: CO2 (Carbon dioxide), SO3 (Sulfur trioxide).
Hydroxides (Bases)Derived from the hydration of a basic oxide:
Basic Oxide + H2O → Hydroxide		Characterized by the hydroxyl group (OH-).
Examples: Mg(OH)2 (Magnesium hydroxide), Ca(OH)2 (Calcium hydroxide).
Acids (Oxyacids and Hydracids)Oxyacids: Anhydride + H2O
Hydracids: Non-metal + Hydrogen (HnX)		Oxyacid: H2CO3 (Carbonic acid)
Hydracid: HCl (Hydrochloric acid)
SaltsResulting from the neutralization reaction:
Acid + Hydroxide → Salt + H2O		Neutral ionic compounds.
Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O (Sodium chloride).

Brønsted-Lowry Definition: An acid is a chemical species capable of donating a proton (H+), while a base is a chemical species capable of accepting a proton (H+).

MIXTURES AND DISPERSED SYSTEMS

A mixture is a chemical-physical system constituted by the coexistence of two or more pure substances that do not react with each other. Dispersed systems, defined by the presence of a dispersing phase (continuous) and a dispersed phase, are classified according to the degree of dispersion and thermodynamic homogeneity:

Polyphasic
Suspensions and Emulsions
→ Heterogeneous Systems (> 1 µm)
Thermodynamically or kinetically unstable systems. Suspensions (solid in liquid) and emulsions (immiscible liquids O/W and W/O) maintain defined interfaces between phases.
Micro-Heterogeneous
Colloidal Systems
→ Colloidal Dispersions (1 - 1000 nm)
Expose a high surface area and prolonged kinetic stability. They exhibit optical properties such as the Tyndall effect and are divided into lyophilic and lyophobic.
Monophasic
True Solutions
→ Molecular Dispersion (< 1 nm)
Thermodynamically stable homogeneous systems in which the solute is totally dissolved in the solvent until the solubility limit and saturation equilibrium are reached.

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Association Colloids and Formulative Example

Association colloids are generated by the spontaneous self-aggregation of amphipathic molecules (surfactants) featuring a hydrophilic polar head and a hydrophobic nonpolar tail. Upon reaching the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), these molecules organize into micelles, reducing the free energy of the system.

In colloidal phase transitions, a distinction is made between GELS (high-viscosity biphasic systems with a continuous three-dimensional network) and SOLS (fluid colloidal suspensions).

Formulative Example (O/W Moisturizing Cream): The structured emulsifying network (Polyglyceryl-4-Stearate, Cetearyl Glucoside) stabilizes the interface of the O/W system. Amphiphilic consistency agents, such as Cetyl Alcohol, and lipid factors like Cera Alba modify the rheology and final texture of the formulation.

The chemical-physical behavior of mixtures and the rheological response of colloidal systems constitute the applicative basis for the development of stable cosmetic-pharmaceutical preparations and formulations.

pH: DEFINITION, THERMODYNAMICS, AND BIOLOGICAL IMPORTANCE 🧬

In summary: pH measures the thermodynamic activity of hydronium ions in solution. Maintaining pH within narrow physiological ranges is fundamental for protein stability, metabolic reactions, and cellular and cutaneous homeostasis.

The pH (potential of hydrogen) is a logarithmic scale (where each 1-unit change represents a 10-fold shift in acidity) quantifying the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution. It is thermodynamically defined as the negative decimal logarithm of the activity of hydronium ions (H3O+):

pH = -log10(aH3O+) = -log10(γ · [H3O+])

Where γ is the activity coefficient (a correction factor for particle interactions; in dilute solutions it is ≈ 1). In very dilute solutions (γ → 1), activity approximates molar concentration: pH ≈ -log10[H3O+]. It reflects the dynamic equilibrium regulated by the ion product of water (Kw).

SCALE AND CLASSIFICATION

pH < 7
Acidic Environment
[H3O+] > [OH−]
Species capable of donating protons (H+). Strength depends on the acid dissociation constant (Ka) and pKa = -log10(Ka).
  • Strong Acids (pKa < 0): Complete dissociation in water (e.g., HCl, HNO3).
  • Weak Acids (pKa > 0): Partial equilibrium; protonated and ionized forms coexist depending on pH (e.g., Citric Acid, AHAs).
pH = 7
Neutrality Point
Pure water at 25°C
H3O+ activity exactly equals OH− activity ([H3O+] = [OH−] = 10-7 M).
  • Ion Product: Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 10-14 at 25°C.
  • Thermal Dependence: At body temperature (37°C), Kw increases and neutrality shifts to pH ~6.81.
pH > 7
Alkaline / Basic Environment
[H3O+] < [OH−]
Species capable of accepting protons (H+) or releasing hydroxyls (OH−). Regulated by the pKb constant.
  • Strong Bases: Complete dissociation with direct release of OH− (e.g., NaOH, KOH).
  • Weak Bases: Partial deprotonation of the solvent to establish basic equilibrium (e.g., Triethanolamine, Ammonia).

BIOLOGICAL RELEVANCE AND HOMEOSTASIS

The human body, composed of 60–70% water, requires strict control of ionic concentrations. A physiological blood pH of approximately 7.4 (range 7.35–7.45) is essential to preserve electrical charge, native conformation, and the functionality of structural and enzymatic proteins.

At the subcellular level, pH compartmentation governs metabolic pathways: the endo-lysosomal system requires progressive acidification down to values of pH 4.5–5.0 to activate acidic hydrolases responsible for degrading molecular debris.

SKIN pH, EUDERMIA, AND BIOLOGICAL DEFENSE 🛡️

The application of topical preparations interacts with the stratum corneum and the hydrolipid film. Maintaining eudermia means respecting the physiological acid gradient to protect barrier function and prevent irritative phenomena.

Epidermal Acid Mantle
Body Skin
pH 4.5 – 6.0 (Average: 5.5)
Acid matrix formed by sebum, sweat (Lactic Acid), and NMF (Natural Moisturizing Factor) substances.
  • Lipid Synthesis: Activates β-glucocerebrosidase for ceramide production.
  • Desmosomal Lysis: Regulates serine proteases (KLK5/KLK7) for physiological desquamation.
Annexial Acid Mantle
Scalp
pH 4.2 – 5.0
Follicular microenvironment with high glandular density.
  • Cuticle Integrity: Prevents swelling of shaft keratin.
  • Microbiome Control: Inhibits hyper-proliferation of Malassezia spp. (a fungus naturally present on the scalp, often linked to dandruff).

CONSEQUENCES OF SKIN pH ALTERATIONS

Neutral-Alkaline Shift (pH ≥ 6.0)
Virulence Switch and Dysbiosis
Alteration of surface charges and inactivation of lipid synthesis enzymes.
  • Acne Pathogenesis: Upregulation of lipases in Cutibacterium acnes.
  • Pathogenic Colonization: Proliferation of Staphylococcus aureus and loss of corneal cohesion.
Excessive Acidification (pH < 4.5)
Irritation and Barrier Damage
Exceeding the physiological skin buffering capacity.
  • Symptomatology: Triggering of erythema, neuropathic burning, and pruritus.
  • Structural Damage: Superficial protein denaturation and suppression of commensal flora.

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Analytical Adjustment and % w/w Stock Solutions

To correct pH in the laboratory, one must operate under constant agitation by adding adjusting solutions drop by drop. To ensure analytical reproducibility regardless of thermal variations, reagents must be prepared strictly on a weight/weight (% w/w) basis totaling 100 g:

  • Citric Acid 20% (w/w): 20 g of Citric Acid + 80 g of Purified Water (Hydrophilic acidifier).
  • Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) 10-18% (w/w): 10–18 g of NaOH + Purified water q.s. to 100 g (Corrosive: handle with PPE).
  • Sodium Bicarbonate 5-10% (w/w): Weak buffer solution for controlled raises up to pH ~8.3.

pH AND HAIR: ELECTROSTATICS, CUTICLE, AND INCI REGULATIONS 💇

ISOELECTRIC POINT AND SURFACE CHARGE

The health of the hair shaft is regulated by the net electrical charge of keratin. Hair exhibits a deep isoelectric point (pI) (the pH at which the net electrical charge of hair is zero, making it less reactive) between 3.67 and 4.5 and a surface iso-charge point at pH ~5.0.

Physiological pH (4.5 – 5.5)
Closed Cuticle and Shine
Minimal net charge state on the shaft surface.
  • Scale Adhesion: Maintains a compact and airtight structure protecting the cortex.
  • Optical-Mechanical Properties: Reduces inter-fiber friction and maximizes light reflection.
Alkaline pH (> 7.0)
Electrostatic Repulsion and Swelling
Deprotonazione dei gruppi carbossilici (-COOH) e tiolici della cheratina.
  • Negative Charge Generation: Repulsion between scales forces them open.
  • Structural Damage: Water swelling (swelling), frizzy effect, and high vulnerability to breakage.

INCI REGULATIONS AND RAW MATERIAL CLASSIFICATION

Under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, ingredient declaration on labels follows well-defined quantitative rules:

FUNCTIONAL CLASSES OF INGREDIENTS

  • Surfactants: Anionic, cationic, amphoteric, and non-ionic for cleansing and wetting.
  • Emulsifiers: Lipophilic/hydrophilic agents for O/W or W/O interface stabilization.
  • Rheology Modifiers: Polymers and hydrocolloid gums for viscosity and yield stress management.
  • Humectants: Hygroscopic polyols (Glycerin, Glycols) for free water retention.
  • Lipids and Emollients: Oils, butters, esters, and silicones for lipid fraction restoration.
  • Sequestering Agents (Chelators): Complexing agents (EDTA, Phytic Acid) for neutralizing metal cations and preventing oxidation.

Hair Formulations: Chemistry and Functionality 💇‍♀️

Cosmetic ingredients can be of mineral, animal, plant, or synthetic origin (obtained in the laboratory through controlled chemical reactions), which currently constitute the majority of components to ensure stability and reproducibility.

USA Approach

American Philosophy

Historically oriented toward stability, sensory pleasantness, and performance, favoring the use of high-performance synthetic or mineral ingredients.
EU Regulation 1223/2009

European Philosophy

Adopts the precautionary principle (a cautionary approach limiting substances before they cause harm), with strict regulations on toxicological safety, sustainability, and biodegradability.

Role of Denatured Alcohol

Denatured alcohol (ethanol rendered unfit for food use via denatonium benzoate) is a ubiquitous component (omnipresent in formulas) with three main technological functions:

Solvent

Solvent Action

Dissolves resins, fats, and water-insoluble organic substances.
Delivery

Excipient & Carrier

Facilitates the penetration of actives into the shaft and provides a rapid sensation of freshness through evaporation.
Hygiene & Viscosity

Antiseptic & Co-solvent

Reduces microbial load and lowers viscosity in gels, improving their fluidity.

Sprays, Lacquers, and Propellants

Modern propellants for atomizing the product are light hydrocarbons (Butane, Isobutane, Propane), which have replaced CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, old atmospheric-damaging gases) banned by the Montreal Protocol. Modern propellants have an ODP (Ozone Depletion Potential) = 0, although they are classified as VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds) with a potential impact on global warming.

In hairsprays, alongside alcohols, volatile solvents (e.g., ethers or acetates) are used to facilitate rapid evaporation and film formation. Chlorinated solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) are now almost absent due to their high toxicity.

Functional Additives, Preservatives, and Strengtheners

Biochem & Formulation
  • Vitamins (Niacinamide - Vit. B₃): Precursor of NAD/NADP coenzymes, essential for cellular energy metabolism and ceramide synthesis (the lipid "bricks" of hair), reinforcing the barrier and shine.
  • Panthenol (Provitamin B₅): On the scalp, it converts into pantothenic acid (a component of Coenzyme A); on the hair shaft, it acts as a powerful hygroscopic humectant (attracting and retaining water), improving hydration, elasticity, and mechanical resistance.
  • Preservatives and Boosters: Use of short/long-chain parabens within legal limits (e.g., butylparaben max 0.14% according to EU Reg.). Propylene Glycol acts as a humectant and preservative system booster by reducing available water activity (aw) for bacteria.

Gels, Foams, and Fixing Power

Gels are high-polymer fixatives in aqueous/alcoholic bases, while Mousses (foams) offer a lighter fixative thanks to their aerated structure.

  • Fatty Excipients: Plant derivatives (e.g., castor oil) added to impart plasticity (flexibility) to the film and reduce the "crust" effect (the rigid flaky film).
  • Thickening Agents (Gums): Cellulose derivatives (Hydroxyethylcellulose, Hydroxypropylcellulose) increase the viscosity of the aqueous phase, stabilize the foam, and enhance fixing action.

Film-Forming Agents and the Natural Effect

Film-formers are polymers (chains of molecules) that form a continuous film on the shaft, imparting body, consistency, and glide. Technology has evolved from rigid polymers to hybrid systems.

Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP): Historical hydrophilic polymer (water-loving). Creates a rigid, crystalline, water-soluble film. Responsible for the classic wet look and "crust" sensation in high humidity.

Modern Systems (PVP + Silicone): The addition of Polydimethylsiloxane (silicone) creates a hydrophobic outer layer (repelling water) that protects PVP from atmospheric humidity. Maintains hold without a wet look, ensuring a natural look and combability.

In mousses, to stabilize foam and aid distribution, a silicone copolymer (e.g., Dimethicone Copolyol) is often used. The hydrophilic polyether component makes it water/alcohol soluble, while the silicone portion imparts shine and reduces tackiness.

Warnings for Fixatives and Trichorrhexis

Excessive use of gels or hairsprays, especially on fragile or chemically treated hair, can stiffen the shaft, making it susceptible to mechanical fracture. Aggressive removal (dry brushing) of polymeric residues can cause Trichorrhexis Nodosa (fracture and fraying of the hair with a typical "brush-like" appearance). Fixatives must always be removed with a gentle wash in lukewarm water, never dry mechanically.

Hair Dyes: Chemical Classification

Coloration is based on the selective absorption of light by chromophoric molecules. Dyes are classified by action mechanism and persistence:

TemporaryHigh molecular weight molecules (large color molecules unable to enter the hair) only on the surface.Removable at the 1st shampoo.
Direct (Semi-permanent)Small molecules with light cortical penetration without oxidation (without chemical reactions with peroxide).Duration: 6-8 washes.
Demi-permanentLow development oxidative system (low hydrogen peroxide), penetrates without lightening.Duration: 20-25 washes.
Permanent (Oxidative)Colorless precursors + H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide) + alkalizing agent (e.g., ammonia) form insoluble pigments.Permanent and stable modification.

HAIR COLORATION MECHANISMS 🎨

Henna (Natural Substantive Coloration)

Unlike oxidative dyes, henna does not use aggressive alkalizing agents. Its active pigment, lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), diffuses through the cuticle and binds stably to keratin via covalent bonds established through a Michael addition reaction with the thiol and amino groups of the hair. The molecule's fixation rate is optimized by warm temperatures and a moderately acidic environment.

  • Coloring Agent: Lawsone, extracted from Lawsonia inermis leaves.
  • Structural Effect: Creates a translucent protective layer that increases stem diameter, mechanical resistance, and shine, sealing cuticles without affecting the internal protein structure.

In addition to its chromatic function, lawsone offers strong sebum-regulating, antifungal, and antibacterial properties. Hair appears more bodied and hydrated, with better-defined curls and a reinforced protective barrier against thermal and environmental stressors.

Pure Henna

100% Lawsonia Inermis

Does not prevent the use of dark or tone-on-tone chemical dyes. However, the lawsone film reduces the absorption of new pigments and makes bleaching or lightening nearly impossible, which will inevitably turn bright orange.
Metallic Salts

Incompatibilità & Rischio

Warning: If the mixture contains sodium picramate or added metallic salts, the reaction with hydrogen peroxide from chemical dyes or lighteners causes hair overheating, immediate fiber breakage, and green shifts.
Phase 2

Temporary Coloration (Rinsing)

Temporarily modifies tone by imparting only reflections. Does not cover gray hair.

  • Mechanism: Pigments with high molecular weight (large color molecules) deposited via physical and electrostatic adsorption. REMOVAL: 1-2 washes.
  • Composition: Absence of ammonia and oxidants; uses direct colorants (azo, anthraquinone).
Phase 3

Direct / Semi-permanent Coloration

Partially covers grays and lasts 4-6 weeks (6-12 washes). Does not lighten.

  1. Penetration: Medium molecules penetrate the cuticle/surface cortex at neutral or slightly acidic pH (5.5–7.0).
  2. Fixation: Retained by Van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds (weak chemical interactions).
▼
Phase 4

Greater penetration into the cortex (lasts 24-28 washes). Uses ethanolamine (a milder alkalizing agent than ammonia) and low-volume H2O2 (1.9% - 4%) (diluted hydrogen peroxide) at pH 7.5–8.5. Reduced concentration of precursors and couplers (resorcinol). Ammonia-free.
Phase 5

Permanent Coloration (Oxidative)

Permanent modification of the chromatic structure.
Two-Step Mechanism:
  1. Alcalinization (pH 9–10): Ammonia/MEA opens cuticles (hair scales). H2O2 irreversibly dissolves natural melanin.
  2. Chromogenesis: Precursors (PPD) + couplers (resorcinol) penetrate and form large molecules (indamines) trapped within the fiber.
A final acidifying treatment is necessary to re-close the cuticles.

CRITICAL INGREDIENTI and Restricted Substances (EC Reg. 1223/2009) 🛑

HAIR SHAMPOO: Function and Composition 🧼

Shampoo is a complex aqueous colloidal system. Its primary function is the mechanical removal of sebum and dirt through the synergistic action of surfactants, without altering the physiological barrier of the scalp.

Formulative Matrix and Functional Roles

A standard formulation consists predominantly of deionized water (70-80%) as a universal solvent and a surfactant system (10-15%) responsible for cleansing. To these, critical functional components for product stability and tolerability are added.

  • Surfactant System: A balanced blend of primary (cleansing) and secondary (softening) surfactants. (See following table for chemical classification and charges).
  • Chelating Agents (Sequestering Agents): Molecules like EDTA or citrates are essential for binding calcium and magnesium ions present in hard water. Without them, surfactants would precipitate, reducing foam and leaving opaque residues on the hair.
  • Buffer System (pH): Additives like citric acid or lactic acid maintain the product at pH 4.5–5.5. This range is crucial for respecting the acid mantle of the scalp and keeping hair cuticles closed and shiny.
  • Rheological Modifiers: Salts (sodium chloride) or cellulosic polymers that increase solution viscosity, improving product handling during application.
  • Preservative System: Necessary given the high water percentage and presence of organic nutrients. Prevents microbial contamination (bacteria and molds) during product shelf life.
  • Conditioning Agents: Polymers or silicones that deposit a thin film onto the fiber. (The electrostatic deposition mechanism is covered in the next block).
  • Esthetic Additives: Perfumes, colorants, and opacifying agents (e.g., glycol distearate) imparting pearlescent appearance and characteristic scent, without direct influence on cleansing.

Surfactant Classes and Electrical Charge

Classification of surfactants by electrical charge, chemical example, and functional role
TypeNet ChargeChemical ExampleFunctional Role
AnionicNegative (-)Sodium Laureth Sulfate (SLES), SLSPrimary cleansing and abundant foam. Can be aggressive if unbalanced.
Amphoteric (Zwitterionic)Variable (pH-dependent)Cocamidopropyl BetaineSofteners and foam stabilizers. At physiological pH (5.5) they reduce anion irritation.
Non-IonicNeutral (0)Decyl Glucoside, AlkanolamidesUltra-delicate cleansing, co-surfactants for sensitive skin. Excellent tolerability.
CationicPositive (+)Cetrimonium Chloride, PolyquaterniumConditioners and antistatics. Non-cleansing: bind to negatively charged keratin.

Cleansing Mechanism (Micellar Dynamics)

Surfactants are amphipathic molecules featuring a hydrophobic (lipophilic) tail and a polar hydrophilic head. Dirt removal follows a well-defined sequential process:

  1. Phase 1: Amphipathic Orientation

    Lipophilic Interaction

    In aqueous environments, surfactant hydrophobic tails orient toward sebum and lipid debris deposited on the fiber or skin.
  2. ▼
  3. Phase 2: CMC Threshold & Aggregation

    Micelle Formation

    Once the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC) is exceeded, molecules self-assemble into spherical (or cylindrical/"vermicelli") aggregates, enclosing dirt at the center.
  4. ▼
  5. Phase 3: Mechanical Removal

    Emulsification & Rinsing

    External hydrophilic heads interact with rinse water, allowing complete solubilization and removal of the hydrophobic micellar structure.

Curative Shampoos (Anti-dandruff and Anti-seborrheic)

Special formulations containing active ingredients with specific actions to normalize cellular turnover or combat microbial proliferation (Malassezia spp.).

Anti-dandruff (Antifungals and Cytostatics):
Utilize active ingredients permitted by the EU Cosmetic Regulation such as Piroctone Olamine and Climbazole. Zinc Pyrithione is banned in the EU as a CMR 1B substance. In exclusively pharmacological settings (OTC or prescription medicines), Ketoconazole or Selenium Disulfide are used instead.
Note: Coal tars are banned in the EU; vegetable oils (Cade, Birch) are used instead for keratolytic and antipruritic action.
Anti-seborrheic:
  • Gentle Cleansers: Non-ionic or amphoteric surfactants (e.g., glucose derivatives) that cleanse without excessively stripping the hydrolipid film, preventing reactive seborrhea.
  • Sebum-Regulating Actives: Ingredients like Zinc PCA or plant extracts (e.g., Serenoa Repens) that modulate 5-alpha-reductase activity, reducing sebum production.

Silicones in Cosmetics

Silicones (silicon-oxygen based inorganic polymers, e.g., Dimethicone, Cyclomethicone) form a breathable occlusive film on the hair surface. This reduces friction (combability), imparts shine, and protects against humidity. They are chemically inert, hypoallergenic, and non-irritating.

The key distinction is between volatile (cyclic) and non-volatile (linear) silicones.
Regulations: Regulation (EU) 2024/1328 on restrictions of cyclic silicones D4, D5, and D6 in rinse-off products is in full effect. The intervention targets the bioaccumulative and persistent (PBT/vPvB) environmental profile rather than human health toxicity.
Comedogenicity: Modern silicones (e.g., high molecular weight dimethicone) are generally non-comedogenic since their macromolecules are too large to clog hair follicles.

POST-SHAMPOO PRODUCTS: Conditioning and Chemical-Functional Treatment 🧴

1. Conditioning Balms (Conditioners)

Formulations designed to restore the tribological properties of the hair fiber, increasing elasticity, cuticular smoothness, shine, and combability (reduction of dynamic friction forces) and neutralizing surface electrostatic charges. Systems indicated for xerotic, chemically treated, or structurally damaged fibers.

  • Composition (Interfacial Phase): Linear chain fatty alcohols acting as co-emulsifiers and structuring agents (e.g., Cetearyl Alcohol), amphipathic cationic surfactants (long-chain alkyl quaternary ammonium salts such as Behentrimonium Chloride or Cetrimonium Chloride), high molecular weight silicone polymers (dimethicone and functionalized amodimethicone), synthetic emollient esters, low molecular weight hydrolyzed proteins (microencapsulated for stabilization and facilitated delivery), and substantive film-forming polymers.
  • Chemical-Physical Mechanism (Molecular Insight): Positive charges of the conditioner bind via electrostatic attraction to free anionic sites (ionized carboxyl groups COO- of aspartic and glutamic acid residues) of exposed keratin. Keratin's isoelectric point (pH ~ 3.7) is altered by alkaline treatments or washing, increasing the negative charge density that this system saturates, favoring alignment and cuticular closure.
  • Persistence and Kinetics: Predominantly reversible surface interaction; the conditioning film is subject to desorption and progressive kinetic removal via subsequent washes with anionic surfactants.
  • Dermatological Contraindications: If applied near the follicular ostium or on seborrheic-prone scalp, they can induce surface buildup (wash-resistant deposition) and accelerate capillary migration of fluid sebum along the shaft via capillarity.

2. Nourishing Masks (Hair Masks)

Emulsified systems with high viscosity and pseudoplastic rheological consistency, formulated for topical post-shampoo applications with prolonged contact times (5-15 minutes). Aimed at the structural restoration of the Cellular Membrane Complex (cuticular CMC) and deep lipid integration of the outer hydrophobic layer.

Colloidal Structure: Predominantly oil-in-water (O/W) emulsions organized in liquid-crystal lamellar phases, stabilized by high-HLB ethoxylated non-ionic surfactants (polysorbates) or biodegradable ester-structured cationic surfactants (esterquats, such as dialkyl ester quaternary ammonium salts).

Over-conditioning Pathophysiology: Hyper-frequent application or inadequate thermal rinsing saturates cuticular porosity, causing rheological fiber heaviness, loss of natural volume, and early onset of surface oiliness due to coalescence of applied lipids with endogenous sebum (greasy effect).

3. Styling Lotions

Topical leave-in formulations engineered to deposit on the cuticle and create transient inter-fiber bridges via synthetic homopolymeric or bio-based film-formers (e.g., PVP, VP/VA Copolymer, vinyl acetate derivatives, or modified polysaccharide polymers). They act by temporarily modifying structural rigidity and imparting geometric shape memory to the styling.
Chemical-Physical Note: Overdosing or ultra-rapid solvent evaporation alters the cohesion of the polymeric film relative to the keratin substrate, causing flaking (microscopic fracture of the film into visible whitish scales, macroscopically confusable with dandruff desquamation).

4. Functional Leave-in Treatments

Hydroalcoholic, hydroglycolic, or microemulsion leave-in solutions applied to the pilosebaceous unit or lengths, designed to act as a vehicle for prolonged release and transcutaneous absorption of target active ingredients.

  • Anti-dandruff & Turnover

    Antimicrobial Lotions

    Ensure prolonged contact for actives compliant with Reg. 1223/2009 (Piroctone Olamine against Malassezia furfur, Climbazole, and keratolytic Salicylic Acid). Formulations free of Zinc Pyrithione (CMR 1B) to avoid hypersensitivity responses.
  • Anti-seborrheic & Sebum Control

    Lipogenesis Modulators

    Reduce sebum synthesis at the ostium using Colloidal Sulfur, Azeloglicine (5-alpha-reductase inhibitor), lipophilic BHAs, and astringent/soothing plant extracts (Sage, Nettle, Aloe vera).
Anti-hair Loss Co-adjuvants & Trichogenic Focus

Follicular Stimulation and DHT Block

Advanced systems to extend the Anagen phase and counteract androgenetic miniaturization. Utilize biomimetic peptide complexes, microcirculatory/VEGF stimulants (Caffeine, Nicotinates, Biotin), and local DHT inhibition via 5-alpha-reductase isoenzyme blockade (e.g., phytosterols from Serenoa repens).
