PIGMENTATION ANOMALIES (DYSCHROMIAS) 🔬

Melanin, synthesized by melanocytes (dendritic cells of the basal layer), is the biological pigment responsible for skin phototype. Dyschromias are qualitative or quantitative alterations of normal pigmentation, classified into hypochromias (pigment deficit) and hyperchromias (pigment excess).

Hyperchromias (Melanodermias)

They are distinguished into generalized forms (correlated with systemic diseases such as Addison's disease, hemochromatosis, or specific vitamin deficiencies) or localized ones.

Freckles (Efelidi):
  • Characteristics: Yellow-brown macules, flat, with blurred margins, typical of light phototypes (I-II).
  • Etiology: Induced by exposure to UV rays; characterized by an increase in tyrosinase activity and melanosome volumetric index, without an increase in the number of melanocytes.
  • Course: Present a marked seasonal cyclicity (accentuated in summer, partially regressing in winter). They show no potential for neoplastic transformation.
Solar Lentigo (Actinic / Senile Lentigo):
  • Characteristics: Flat macules (not raised), hyperpigmented, with sharp margins ("stamped-out"). Unlike freckles, they persist stably throughout the year and are a chronic expression of photoaging (cumulative actinic damage).
  • Histopathology: Linear and focal hyperplasia of melanocytes arranged along the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Treatment Approach: Focused cryotherapy, laser therapy (Q-switched/Picoseconds), or topical protocols with depigmenting agents.
Melanocytic Nevi (Acquired Nevus):

Benign melanocytic proliferation organized into nests of nevus cells. They are classified based on histological site into: junctional (flat), compound (moderately raised), or dermal (tuberosus or papillomatous). Dysplastic (atypical) nevi require close clinical monitoring due to the risk of evolution or simulation of malignant melanoma.

Clinical Protocol: ABCDE Rule for Melanoma Screening

Dermoscopy

Clinical monitoring parameters:
- A - Asymmetry: Lesion not superimposable on its two axes.
- B - Borders: Irregular, notched, or geographic map-like.
- C - Color: Variable, polychrome (brown, black, red, white, blue).
- D - Diameter: Greater than 6 mm.
- E - Evolution: Rapid changes in shape, size, color, or symptoms.
Additional semiological signs: spontaneous bleeding, localized pruritus, onset of a peri-lesional erythematous halo (Meyerson's sign).

Other Localized Hyperchromias:
Melasma (including pregnancy chloasma of hormonal etiopathogenesis), actinic lentigo, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), and tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor) in its hyperchromic manifestation.

Hypochromias (Leucodermias)

Clinical conditions characterized by a marked reduction or total absence of melanin synthesis.

Vitiligo:
  • Etiology: Chronic autoimmune pathology characterized by the selective destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+), on a basis of strong genetic predisposition (polygenic clusters).
  • Clinical: Achromic macules (milky white color) with sharp, hyperpigmented margins, frequently symmetrical distribution. The appearance of leucotrichia (whitening of hairs within the lesion) indicates involvement of the follicular melanocytic reservoir, configuring an unfavorable prognostic sign.
  • Management and Risks: Achromic skin is completely devoid of natural barrier against ultraviolet (UV) radiation (high risk of sunburn and actinic carcinogenesis). Topical broad-spectrum photoprotection (SPF 50+) is mandatory.
Oculocutaneous Albinism (OCA):
  • Etiology: Heterogeneous group of genetic disorders with autosomal recessive transmission, characterized by the total or partial absence of melanin synthesis. Melanocytes are microscopically present but biochemically non-functional due to a congenital enzymatic deficit (e.g., tyrosinase gene mutation for OCA1 or other genes in the biosynthetic pathway).
  • Clinical: Achromic skin, white or straw-blond hair and body hair, translucent gray-blue irises with a typical red pupillary reflex in transillumination.
  • Ocular Complications: Foveal hypoplasia (failure of anatomical development of the central fovea), congenital nystagmus (involuntary oscillatory eye movements), severe photophobia due to lack of iris pigment shielding, strabismus, and low vision due to altered decussation of optic nerve fibers at the chiasm.
Other Hypochromias:
Pityriasis alba (common hypochromic manifestation in subjects with atopic dermatitis), tinea versicolor in its post-infective hypochromic phase, nevus anemicus (congenital defect of vascular adrenergic receptors), and idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (typical of chronological aging of the limbs).

CUTANEOUS ELEMENTARY LESIONS: Classification and Diagnosis 🔬

Elementary lesions represent the fundamental morphological and anatomo-pathological unit of cutaneous response to endogenous or exogenous insults. Dermatological diagnosis is based on systematic analysis of their morphology, extension, configuration, topographical distribution, and spatial arrangement.

Start / Healthy Skin
Primitive Lesions
Primary and direct manifestations of the cutaneous pathological process arising on healthy skin.
Examples: Macule, papule, plaque, nodule, wheal, vesicle, bulla, pustule.
Evolution / Traumatic Insult
Secondary Lesions
Expression of the natural evolution of primitive lesions or physical/mechanical insults.
Examples: Scale, crust, excoriation, erosion, ulceration, fissure, scar.
Polymorphic Coexistence
Primitive-Secondary Frameworks
Simultaneous presence of primitive lesions in active phase and secondary ones in evolutionary phase/outcome (e.g., Eczema/Dermatitis: erythema, edema, and vesicles coexist with excoriations and lichenification).

Primitive Lesions (Initial)

Vascular Dynamics
Erythema
Redness from vasodilation of the superficial dermal plexus. Positive diascopy (disappears with vitropressure).
Frameworks: Infectious exanthems, solar erythema, rosacea.
Pigmentary / Hemorrhagic
Macule / Patch
Non-palpable modification of skin color. Negative diascopy. Hyperchromic, hypochromic, or hemorrhagic (purpora, petechiae).
Nomenclature: Macule (≤ 1 cm), Patch (> 1 cm).
Solid Superficial
Papule / Plaque
Solid and raised lesion. Papule (≤ 1 cm), Plaque (> 1 cm). Derives from epidermal hyperplasia or inflammatory infiltrate.
Examples: Lichen planus, psoriasis.
Solid Deep
Nodule / Nodosity
Nodule (> 1 cm, mid-deep dermis). Nodosity (deep infiltrative dermo-hypodermal process, e.g., erythema nodosum).
Transient Edematous
Wheal
Acute edema of the papillary dermis mediated by histamine. Transient (< 24h), associated with intense pruritus.
Examples: Urticaria, insect bites.
Serous / Purulent
Vesicle / Bulla / Pustule
Fluid collections: Vesicle (≤ 5 mm), Bulla (> 5 mm, phlycten). Pustule (septic or aseptic purulent exudate).

Secondary Lesions (Evolutionary)

Hyperkeratosis
Scale
Visible accumulation of corneal lamellae (pityriasic, psoriatic, lamellar). Indicator of altered keratinization or parakeratosis.
Drying
Crust
Drying of serum, blood, or pus (serum-hematic, meliceric, purulent). Temporarily substitutes the damaged epithelium.
Superficial (No Scar)
Excoriation / Erosion
Excoriation (traumatic/scratching origin, epidermis only). Erosion (pathological origin). Both re-epithelialize without a scar.
Deep (With Scar)
Ulceration / Fissure
Ulceration (loss of substance down to dermis/hypodermis). Fissure (linear cleft in tension zones). Resolve with a scar.
Reparative Outcome
Scar
Newly formed fibrous-collagenous tissue devoid of skin appendages. Forms: normotrophic, atrophic, hypertrophic, keloid.
Differential diagnosis: Simple skin atrophy preserves residual appendages, absent in true scar.

HAIR SHAFT ANOMALIES: FRACTURES AND STRUCTURAL DEFORMITIES 💔

Hair shaft anomalies are structural alterations that compromise the mechanical resistance of the keratin fiber, classified based on the location of damage (cuticle, cortex, medulla) and etiology (acquired/traumatic vs. genetic/congenital).

Acquired Fracture
Trichorrhexis Nodosa (Brush-like)
Focal loss of cuticle and cortical fraying. Whitish nodules with "brush-like" fracture.
Etiology: Cumulative physical-chemical traumas (heat, bleaching, perms).
Congenital / Sulfur Deficit
Trichothiodystrophy (Clean Fracture)
Clean and neat transverse fracture. In polarized microscopy shows alternating "tiger tail" pattern.
Association: Sign of Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) due to cystine deficit.
Pathognomonic
Trichorrhexis Invaginata (Bamboo Hair)
Intussusception deformity: distal segment invaginates into proximal (ball-and-socket junction or "golf head").
Association: Netherton Syndrome (SPINK5 mutation).
Mitotic Arrest
Tapered Hairs (Pencil-point Hairs)
Breakage upon sudden shaft thinning. Tapered proximal fragment (tapered hairs).
Association: Alopecia Areata and anagen dystrophy from chemotherapy.
Physical-Chemical Degradation
Trichoptilosis (Split Ends)
Distal longitudinal fissuring and splitting due to cuticular weathering.
Etiology: Exclusively acquired from mechanical-chemical traumas.
Incomplete Fracture
Trichoclasis (Greenstick Fracture)
Incomplete transverse fracture of cortex and medulla with intact cuticle acting as a bridge (greenstick fracture).
Etiology: Moderate physical traumas or mechanical bending.

ALTERATIONS OF SHAFT REGULARITY AND STRUCTURE 📏

Anomalies of the longitudinal or transverse morphology of the hair. The fundamental clinical distinction lies in the regularity of the defect (often genetic) compared to irregularity (often acquired or traumatic).

Regular Hereditary
Monilethrix (Necklace Hair)
Regular elliptical nodes alternating with thin internodes (where fracture occurs).
Etiology: Keratin gene mutations (KRT81, KRT83, KRT86) or Desmoglein 4 (DSG4).
Acquired Artifact
Pseudomonilethrix
Swellings of irregular amplitude and distance with intact cuticle.
Difference from Monilethrix: Traumatic/mechanical origin, non-hereditary.
Axial Torsion
Pili Torti (Twisted Hairs)
Flattened shaft with 90°–180° twists at irregular intervals. Sparkling reflection (sparkling).
Association: Menkes Syndrome (ATP7A mutation, copper deficiency).
Mitotic Slowdown
Tapered Hairs (Capelli Affusolati)
Progressive narrowing along the shaft with intact cuticle.
Significance: Temporary inhibition of the follicular matrix (Alopecia Areata, trichotillomania).
Triangular Section
Longitudinal Grooves
Presence of longitudinal groove and triangular cross-section.
Pathognomonic: Uncombable Hair Syndrome (UHS), "glass wool" hair.
Air Bands
Pili Annulati (Ringed Hair)
Alternating light and dark bands due to micro-air cavities in the cortex.
Clinical: Hereditary (locus 12q). Hair is not fragile; aesthetic alteration.
Partial Duplication
Pili Bifurcati
The shaft divides into two distinct branches each with its own cuticle.
Mechanism: Temporary formation of a secondary matrix or duplication of the papilla.
Shared Ostium
Pili Multigemini
2–10 distinct shafts emerge from a single follicular ostium.
Differential diagnosis: Distinct from Trichostasis Spinulosa (trapped telogen hairs).

RESIDUAL ANOMALIES AND ALTERATIONS OF SHAFT CURVATURE ➰

This section groups acquired defects from mechanical trauma (knotting) and congenital anomalies altering the cross-sectional geometry or curvature of the shaft, affecting combability and aesthetic appearance without necessarily inducing fracture fragility.

Trichonodosis (Knotted Hair / Trichonodosis)

Definition:
An exclusively acquired anomaly characterized by the formation of true knots along the shaft (single-strand knots). At the loop of the knot, mechanical tension causes cuticular flaking with cortical exposure and fraying.
Pathogenesis and Biomechanics:
Derives from repeated mechanical traumas (aggressive brushing, friction). The highly flattened or elliptical cross-section reduces torsional moment of inertia (i.e., the structural resistance of hair to twist onto itself), favoring self-curling and knotting ("spring effect").
Risk Factors:
Prevalent in individuals with curly, kinky, or very fine hair (African descent or curly Caucasian hair). Rarely spontaneous in extremely long, neglected hair.

Uncombable Hair Syndrome (Uncombable Hair Syndrome - UHS)

Pediatric clinical framework correlated with the microscopic sign of Pili trianguli et canaliculi (triangular cross-section shafts with a longitudinal groove), showing gradual spontaneous resolution during puberty.

Molecular Etiology and UHS Biochemical Cascade

Genetic Pathway

Genetic disease with autosomal recessive inheritance linked to mutations in the follicular keratinization complex: PADI3, TGM3, TCHH, and SULT2B1.

Phase 1: Trichohyalin Deimination
PADI3 → TCHH
Peptidylarginine deiminase 3 (PADI3) deiminates trichohyalin (TCHH), allowing its linkage with keratin filaments.
↓
Phase 2: Isopeptide Cross-Linking
TGM3 (Transglutaminase 3)
Catalyzes stable isopeptide cross-links for structural consolidation.
↓
Pathological Outcome
Premature IRS Keratinization
The axis defect causes premature keratinization of the inner root sheath (IRS), deforming and stiffening the malleable shaft.

Clinical Correlate: Dry, frizzy, outward-projecting hair, impossible to flatten but without significant increase in tensile fragility.

Woolly Hair

Morphology and Differential Diagnosis:
Shafts with ovoid/flattened cross-section, characterized by tight axial torsions and irregular curvatures. Compared to Pili Torti (180° torsions along the longitudinal axis), torsions are less structured and mechanical resistance is largely preserved.
Pathophysiology:
Marked reduction of the anagen phase (active growth phase, with maximum hair length often < 5 cm). Combability restriction is linked to the spatial density of micro-curvatures, not shaft fracture.
Clinical VariantInheritance & GeneticsPathological Features & Associations
Hereditary (Generalized)Autosomal Dominant or RecessiveInvolves the entire scalp. Recessive forms are markers of severely disabling cardio-cutaneous syndromes (e.g., Naxos or Carvajal Syndrome due to desmosomal gene mutations in JUP or DSP).
Localized (Woolly Hair Nevus)Non-hereditaryCircumscribed patch on healthy scalp; sometimes present in mosaicism associated with epidermal nevi.
Acquired (Induced Kinky Hair)Iatrogenic / ReactiveRare, secondary to systemic drugs (retinoids such as acitretin/isotretinoin, EGFR inhibitors) or in early stages of androgenetic alopecia.

SEBORRHEA AND SEBACEOUS DYSFUNCTION 💧

Seborrhea is defined as an increased quantitative production of sebum (seborrhea oleosa) or a qualitative alteration of its lipid composition (seborrhea sicca). It is not an isolated pathology, but a homeostatic dysfunction altering the surface hydrolipid film, creating a suitable microenvironment for acne, dandruff, and seborrheic dermatitis.

Clinical Classification of Seborrhea

Clinical FormPathophysiological MechanismCutaneous Manifestations & Consequences
Physiological SeborrheaBalanced secretory activity of holocrine glands regulated by age, sex, hormones, and genetics.Establishment of the hydrolipid barrier and physiological shaft lubrication.
Pathological Seborrhea (Oleosa)Quantitative hyperproduction of sebum.Hyper-greasy skin and appendages, sebaceous retention (stasis of oxidized sebum), comedones, and microbiota dysbiosis (ecological imbalance).
Dry Seborrhea (Sicca)Qualitative alteration of the lipid fraction: linoleic acid deficit and excess of oxidized squalene.Desquamative and xerotic appearance (pathological skin dryness), despite normo- or hypersecretion of glands.

Pathophysiology and Molecular Mechanisms

Molecular Cascade of Seborrhea

Endocrinology & Microbiome
Endocrine Stimulus
Testosterone → DHT
Synthesis of 5α-dihydrotestosterone via type I 5α-reductase. DHT binds to androgen receptors (AR).
Signaling Enhancement
IGF-1 / Insulin
Activation of the mTORC1 axis amplifying and co-stimulating the lipogenic pathway.
↓
Gene Activation
SREBP-1c Pathway
Transcription of Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein for direct stimulation of lipogenesis in sebocytes.
Lipid Alteration & Peroxidation:
Depletion of linoleic acid (essential for barrier function and inter-keratinocyte cohesion) and relative increase of squalene. Peroxidized squalene (squalene monohydroperoxide) induces a pro-inflammatory state and infundibular hyperkeratosis (thickening of the follicle neck).
Role of Microbiota and Malassezia spp.:
Opportunistic lipophilic yeasts Malassezia restricta and M. globosa metabolize sebaceous triglycerides via extracellular lipases, releasing irritating free fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid). Penetration into the stratum corneum causes inflammation, itching, and reactive desquamation.

Clinical Consequences and Differential Diagnosis

  • Androgenetic Alopecia: Seborrhea acts as a cofactor: perifollicular microinflammation accelerated by lipid peroxides and microbiota amplifies miniaturization of susceptible follicles.
  • Folliculitis and Acne Vulgaris: Microcomedone obstruction creates an anoxic environment ideal for hyper-proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, leading to an inflammatory cascade.
  • Pityriasis Steatoides: Intermediate condition characterized by yellowish, greasy scales adhering to the scalp, soaked in degraded sebum.
  • Seborrheic Dermatitis: Chronic relapsing dermatitis (erythema, scaling, and itching) located in high-sebum areas, driven by interaction between sebum, Malassezia, and host immune response.

Therapeutic Approach and Sebum Regulation

The clinical target includes reducing microbial load, restoring epidermal turnover, and controlling lipogenesis, while protecting skin barrier integrity to prevent rebound effect (compensatory reactive hypersecretion).

Therapeutic ClassActive IngredientsClinical Action Mechanism
Antifungals & AntimicrobialsKetoconazole / Ciclopirox Olamine
Piroctone Olamine / Zinc Pyrithione		Broad spectrum against Malassezia spp.; cytostatic action (cell proliferation blockade) and normalizing effect on skin microbiota.
Keratolytics & Sebum ModulatorsSalicylic Acid / Azelaic Acid
Zinc PCA / Niacinamide		Lipophilic keratolytic action (removal of corneal plugs), anti-inflammatory, 5α-reductase inhibition, and protection against squalene peroxidation.
Physiotherapeutic & Instrumental SupportHigh Frequency
LLLT (Photobiomodulation)		Ozone generation with bactericidal, fungicidal, and vasomodulating action; Low-Level Laser Therapy (LLLT) to attenuate inflammation and stimulate repair.

DANDRUFF (PITYRIASIS SIMPLEX CAPITIS) 🌨️

Dandruff is a chronic non-inflammatory (or mildly inflammatory) condition characterized by visible scalp scaling. It is caused by an accelerated epidermal turnover: keratinocyte renewal time decreases from about 28 days to 2–7 days. Cells do not reach full maturation and aggregate into visible scales before shedding.

Pathophysiology: Etiological Triad and Barrier Damage

Etiopathogenetic Triad of Dandruff

Homeostasis Barrier
1. Excess Sebum (Substrate) + 2. Presence of Malassezia + 3. Individual Susceptibility
Pathogenesis requires simultaneous interaction of all three factors (genetics, immune status, and barrier integrity).
Role of Malassezia:
Dandruff requires the presence of lipophilic yeast Malassezia (species M. globosa and M. restricta). Its lipases hydrolyze sebum triglycerides, releasing free fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid). In susceptible individuals, oleic acid penetrates the stratum corneum, inducing irritation, sub-clinical inflammation, and parakeratosis (persistence of cell nuclei in the stratum corneum due to hyper-proliferation).
Skin Barrier Disruption:
Dandruff-affected stratum corneum exhibits compromised barrier function and increased permeability (elevated TEWL - Transepidermal Water Loss). This favors irritant penetration and dehydration, fueling a vicious cycle of dryness and scaling.

Clinical Classification of Dandruff

VariantScale MorphologyUnderlying Skin StatusClinical Classification
Pityriasis Sicca (Dry)Fine, white or grayish, powdery, loosely adhering.Normal or slightly xerotic (dry). Mild or absent itching.Typical during winter (dry air).
Pityriasis Steatoides (Oily)Large, greasy, yellowish, aggregated in adherent plaques.Erythematous (reddened), oily, and inflamed.Mild form of seborrheic dermatitis; requires more aggressive treatment.

Therapeutic Strategy and Management

The therapeutic goal is to control the Malassezia population, normalize keratinocyte turnover, and reduce inflammation while restoring the skin barrier.

Pharmacological CategoryActive IngredientsSpecific Mechanism of Action
Antifungal Agents- Ketoconazole (2%)
- Zinc Pyrithione (ZPT)
- Ciclopirox Olamina / Selenium Sulfide		Inhibition of ergosterol synthesis (fungal membrane component); fungicidal, antibacterial, and cytostatic activity to reduce keratinocyte hyper-proliferation.
Keratolytic Agents- Salicylic Acid
- Sulfur		Promote chemical desquamation ("unsticking" of scales) and follicular penetration; sebostatic action. They lack direct antifungal activity.
Natural AdjuvantsTea Tree Oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)Demonstrated antifungal activity in clinical studies against Malassezia species.

Correct Use and Chemical-Physical Parameters

Usage Protocol

It is essential to use shampoos with an acidic pH (4.0–5.5) to respect the physiological hydrolipid film and create an unfavorable environment for fungal proliferation (which prefers neutral or alkaline pH).

Contact time is crucial: therapeutic shampoo must act for 3–5 minutes before rinsing. Studies demonstrate that contact times under 2 minutes drastically reduce the antifungal and cytostatic efficacy of active ingredients.

HAIR: HOW IT IS MADE AND ITS LIFE CYCLE

1. ANATOMY AND STRUCTURE OF THE HAIR

Body hair and head hair are filaments made of keratin. They originate from a "sac" in the skin called the HAIR FOLLICLE.

The follicle is located beneath the skin of the scalp (dermis). Its concave end is called the BULB.

The length, thickness, and distribution of hair vary based on location, sex, age, and ethnicity.

Parts of the Hair

  • The part that emerges from the skin is called the SHAFT (or STEM).
  • The part under the skin (inside the follicle) is called the ROOT.
  • At the bottom of the root lies the DERMAL PAPILLA. This papilla delivers nutrients to the hair.
  • Between the bulb and the root is the HAIR MATRIX. The matrix produces all the components of the hair.

These parts form the PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT.

PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT: COMPONENTS

  • ▶ HAIR FOLLICLE (with hair)
  • ▶ ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLE
  • ▶ SEBACEOUS GLAND

HAIR FOLLICLE:

The follicle is an inclined "sac" in the skin that extends 1-3 mm into the dermis. It contains the hair and its sheaths.

Each person has about 5 million follicles. Around 100,000 are on the scalp. This number is set before birth and does not increase.

SEBACEOUS GLAND:

This gland produces sebum, a fatty substance (triglycerides, cholesterol, etc.).

Sebum serves to lubricate, soften, and protect the hair as it grows. It spreads over the skin and hair. Its activity is regulated by hormonal and dietary factors.

ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLE:

It is composed of smooth muscle fibers attached to the follicle.

When it contracts (due to cold or emotions like fear), the hair stands upright, causing goosebumps. It also helps push sebum out.

2. STRUCTURE OF THE HAIR

Hair is a complex fiber containing water (10-30%) and lipids (sebum, waxes, etc.) for protection.

The hair shaft consists of three layers:

  • CUTICLE: The outermost layer. It is made of flat, overlapping cells, like roof tiles.
  • CORTEX: Located beneath the cuticle, it is the largest part of the hair. It provides strength and contains melanin (pigment).
  • MEDULLA: The central core, often absent in fine hair.

The main components are: keratin (structure), melanin (color), and minerals.

KERATIN: THE FUNDAMENTAL STRUCTURE

Hair is primarily made of keratin, present in two forms:

  • Filamentous Keratin: Forms bundles (fibrils) in the cortex.
  • Amorphous Keratin: Fills the spaces between bundles, providing stability.

HOW IS STRUCTURAL STABILITY MAINTAINED?

Keratin chains are held together by "bonds". There are 3 types of bonds:

1. HYDROGEN BONDS

These are very weak bonds that break easily with water or heat, providing flexibility.

2. SALT BONDS

These are moderately strong bonds broken by high heat or acidic/basic conditions, providing strength.

3. DISULFIDE BONDS

These are very strong covalent bonds formed by sulfur atoms.

They determine structure (e.g., naturally curly hair) and can only be broken with significant chemical energy.

All three bond types contribute to overall hair resistance.

MINERALS

Minerals are essential. A deficiency makes hair fragile, dry, and dull.

Key minerals include:

  • IRON: Deficiency causes brittleness and excessive shedding.
  • COPPER: Essential for pigment production (melanin) and disulfide bonds.
  • ZINC: Crucial for cellular growth and repair.

LIPIDS (FATS)

Lipids mainly originate from sebum.

Phospholipids are key to maintaining proper hair hydration.

MELANIN: NATURAL COLOR

Melanin is the natural pigment found in the cortex, produced by melanocytes.

Types of pigment:

  • EUMELANIN: Provides brown/black tones (dark hair).
  • PHEOMELANIN: Provides yellow/red tones (blond and red hair).
  • TRICHOCHROMES: Special pigments responsible for vibrant red shades.

Melanin is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine. The ratio of these pigments determines final hair color.

3. HAIR LIFE CYCLE

Hair goes through repeated growth and resting phases. When an old hair falls out, the follicle generates a new one.

The cycle consists of 3 phases:

1. ANAGEN: Growth phase

The longest phase. The hair matrix is highly active, driving continuous growth.

  • Duration: 2-4 years in men, 3-7 years in women.
  • Hair grows approximately 1-1.5 cm per month.

2. CATAGEN: Transition phase

A very short phase lasting 2-4 weeks, during which growth stops.

3. TELOGEN: Resting phase

The resting period, lasting around 3 months.

The old hair sheds only when pushed out by new emerging hair.

Human hair shedding follows a mosaic pattern: each follicle operates independently, preventing widespread hair loss at once.

Note: Each follicle can undergo up to 30 life cycles.
